reading.body:
Oregon's AI legislation is procurement and companion rules, not data center or grid rules.

Two of the fifteen bills name artificial intelligence directly: SB1546 on AI companions and HB4103 on artificial intelligence generally. A third, SB1587 on data brokers, touches the data layer that feeds models. The rest are the ordinary business of a session, covering state financial administration, batteries, elections, housing, public safety, medical assistance, and journalism compensation. The only executive action in the record is an order setting AI procurement safeguards for state government.

For AI specifically, this is the demand side of the stack being governed before the supply side. Procurement rules decide which models a state buys and under what terms. Companion rules decide what those models may do to users. Neither constrains the compute, the buildings, or the power that determine how much AI Oregon can actually run. A state can write careful purchasing standards and still have no say in whether the interconnection queue moves.

The data does not show whether any bill passed, what the procurement order requires, or how many facilities sit in Oregon. It records titles and dates, not outcomes. Nothing here measures electricity demand, water use, or data center construction, so it cannot support any claim about the grid as a constraint. The two news items are dated September and October 2026, after the legislative dates, and one concerns a multi-state governors group rather than Oregon alone.

The fifteen bills split into two groups by what they can actually reach. Three touch the model layer directly: SB1546 on AI companions, HB4103 on artificial intelligence, and SB1587 on data brokers. The other twelve are the routine business of a session, and their presence in the same list is a reminder that AI legislation competes for floor time with housing, elections, and medical assistance. A state that spends its session on procurement standards and companion rules has spent nothing on the physical layer.

The dates cluster. Eight of the fifteen bills carry April 2026 dates, and the two AI-named bills fall on April 5, the same day as public safety, medical assistance, and economic development measures. That is the shape of a deadline, not a priority ranking. Bills introduced together near a cutoff tell you when they were filed, not how far they moved.

The executive order is the only action in the record that binds state purchasing rather than private conduct. Procurement safeguards govern what Oregon government buys. Companion rules govern what models do to users. Neither category reaches interconnection, land, or generation, which is where the constraint on AI scaling sits. Oregon can set the terms of its own purchases and still have no instrument aimed at whether a facility can get power.

What did Oregon actually pass on AI?
The data does not say. It records bill titles and dates, not outcomes, so no bill in this list can be confirmed as passed or failed.

Which Oregon bills name artificial intelligence directly?
Two: SB1546, relating to artificial intelligence companions, and HB4103, relating to artificial intelligence. Both carry April 5, 2026 dates.

Does Oregon have any legislation on data centers or the grid?
None appears in this data. The fifteen titles cover financial administration, batteries, elections, housing, data brokers, economic development, public safety, AI companions, medical assistance, semi-independent state agencies, journalism compensation, downcoding, artificial intelligence, and a memorial resolution.

What does Oregon's AI executive order require?
The data gives only the headline: it establishes AI procurement safeguards for Oregon government. The text of the order and its specific requirements are not in this record.

How many AI bills has Oregon introduced compared with other states?
The data covers Oregon alone and holds no other state's count, so no comparison is possible from it.

When was this record last updated?
The build timestamp is October 3, 2026, and the page is marked as generated October 4, 2026. The most recent item in it is an October 2, 2026 news story about a bipartisan governors group on AI.
